 A decade of Social Security payments, more than $107,000 in all, landed in the wrong hands because one death never got reported. Federal prosecutors say the money went to the dead woman’s grandson, and now he’s heading to prison.
 That grandson is 55-year-old Jonathan Frank Barner of Illinois, who received a 15-month federal sentence from U.S. District Judge John Badalamenti, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. The court also ordered him to forfeit exactly $107,175, as listed in the announcement.

 Barner pleaded guilty on May 18, 2026. The Justice Department says the theft ran from about May 2013 through April 2023, meaning payments kept arriving for roughly 10 years after they should have stopped.

 Spread across those 120 months, the stolen total works out to about $893 a month. That kind of steady deposit can slip under the radar when nobody tells the government a beneficiary has died.
 Reporting a death to Social Security
 Reporting a death isn’t optional. USAGov says you must notify the Social Security Administration when a beneficiary dies, and the agency accepts those reports only by phone at 1-800-772-1213 or in person.
 But in many cases, a funeral home handles it. The Social Security Administration says funeral directors usually report a death to the agency, which is why families are asked to hand over the deceased person’s Social Security number.
 Don’t assume that step is automatic, though. The agency tells families to contact Social Security as soon as they can, so a missed handoff doesn’t leave payments running.

 What happens to money arriving after a death
 Benefits that show up after a death generally must be returned. Social Security says families must give back any benefits received for the month of death and any later months. The agency notes that if a payment arrived by direct deposit, contact the bank or financial institution, and a paper check shouldn’t be cashed.
 Keeping those payments is a different story from an honest mix-up. Under federal law on stealing government money, the penalty is a fine, up to 10 years in prison or both. Cases where the value is $1,000 or less carry a maximum of one year.
 Unrecovered overpayments are a big problem
 This case is one example of a wider problem. An August 2026 audit from the Social Security Administration’s inspector general found 17,979 adult beneficiaries who died between December 2022 and December 2024 had roughly $240 million in outstanding overpayments.
 The audit found that the agency didn’t follow its recovery policies in 59 of 125 sampled cases, or about 47%. The inspector general estimated about $106 million was owed by 8,486 deceased beneficiaries.

 What families should do after a loss
 If you’re handling a loved one’s affairs, start by giving the funeral director their Social Security number, then confirm with the agency directly. Check their bank account for any deposit that arrives after the date of death, and ask the bank to return it rather than letting it sit.
 And keep a record of every call and letter. If something looks off, such as a payment that keeps coming, call Social Security as soon as possible.
